e: Compare Sanskrit अलाक (alāka, “crown flower; kind of dye”).

From Middle English ald, and from Old English eald.
Preserved in Northern English and Geordie dialects as aald, reflecting older vowel pronunciation and regional phonology.
q: Aald, 'old' – “an aald man” = an elderly man.
2005, Bill Griffiths, A Dictionary of North East Dialect, →ISBN, page 4:
Aald, old. In common use in the Northumbrian and Geordie dialects.
1905, Joseph Wright, The English Dialect Dictionary, volume 1, page 46:

e: From Hawaiian ʻaʻaliʻi (“name of any of the hardwood shrubs of the genus Dodonaea”).
